blocks.text: Water makes up roughly **60% of body weight** in an adult man (a higher share in infants, a lower share in women). In a 70 kg man that is about **40 L**: around **25 L inside cells** and **15 L extracellular**, of which about 12 L is interstitial and only about **3 L is plasma**.

**Sodium concentration is a water problem; total body sodium is a volume problem.** Plasma [Na] sets osmolality and therefore cell volume, so disorders of water show up as **hypo-/hypernatraemia**. Total body Na sets ECF volume, so disorders of salt show up as **hypo-/hypervolaemia**. Aldosterone keeps sodium (water follows it); ADH keeps water alone.

blocks.title: Water balance numbers worth memorising
rows: Urine osmolality the kidney can reach
2 × Na + urea + glucose (Na doubled to account for its anions)

blocks.title: ADH (vasopressin) in brief
items: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense a rise in osmolality → **thirst** plus ADH release from the **posterior pituitary**.
ADH binds **V2 receptors** on collecting-duct cells → **aquaporin-2** channels are inserted into the luminal membrane → water is drawn out along the medullary osmotic gradient.
**Non-osmotic** triggers also release ADH: **hypovolaemia** (whatever the osmolality), stress such as surgery or trauma, pain and **nausea**.
If ADH is absent, the collecting duct stays watertight and dilute urine is passed.

blocks.title: What the kidney needs to dilute or concentrate urine
rows: Solute reaching the loop and early distal tubule; a working loop/early distal tubule; **no ADH** in the blood
Solute delivery and a working loop (to build the medullary gradient); **ADH released**; collecting duct **responds** to ADH

blocks.text: When **measured** osmolality is clearly higher than the **calculated** value (an osmolar gap), suspect an unmeasured osmole such as **ethanol or ethylene glycol**; the gap roughly estimates its concentration.

blocks.title: Common isotonic IV fluids (per litre)
rows: ECF only: about 3/15 stays in plasma
All body water: only about 3/40 stays in plasma

blocks.title: Daily maintenance needs of an adult
Choosing a fluid
items: **Crystalloids** are the resuscitation fluid of choice: albumin gave no advantage and synthetic colloids raised AKI and mortality in the critically ill.
0.9% saline can cause a mild **hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis**; Hartmann's, being slightly hypotonic, can cause mild hyponatraemia.
In critically ill patients, **balanced crystalloids** (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte; less chloride) gave fewer deaths, new dialysis or persistent renal dysfunction than saline.
Large acute salt and water losses: IV 0.9% saline, given fast (around 1 L/hour) if the patient is hypotensive.
**Pure water loss** (e.g. diabetes insipidus) is replaced as water: orally, or IV as 5% dextrose, because plain water infused IV would lyse blood cells.

blocks.text: **5% dextrose does not resuscitate.** The glucose is metabolised and the water spreads through all 40 L of body water, so only about 75 mL of each litre stays in the circulation. Use a crystalloid such as 0.9% saline or Hartmann's for hypovolaemia.

blocks.note: Look at: the countercurrent loop building a medullary gradient up to 1200 mOsmol/kg, fluid leaving the early distal tubule at about 100 mOsmol/kg, and how ADH (water deficit) or its absence (water overload) sets the final urine.

blocks.text: **Hyponatraemia = serum Na < 135 mmol/L.** Whatever the cause, the body has kept **more water than sodium**. It is the commonest biochemical abnormality in hospital, affecting up to about a third of inpatients. Sort the causes by the patient's **ECF volume**: hypovolaemic, euvolaemic or hypervolaemic.

blocks.title: Causes by volume status
rows: Renal: diuretics (**thiazides** above all), adrenal failure. GI: vomiting, diarrhoea. Skin: burns
Water gain with normal body sodium
Primary polydipsia; electrolyte-free IV fluid (e.g. post-op 5% dextrose, bladder irrigation fluid at prostatectomy); **SIADH**; hypothyroidism
Salt and water both retained, water more so
Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, CKD with continued free-water intake

blocks.title: Severity and symptoms (Davidson)
rows: Vomiting, drowsiness, seizures, coma, cardiorespiratory arrest

blocks.text: **Speed matters more than the number.** A fast fall in osmolality drives water into neurons, causing **cerebral oedema**. If the fall is slow, neurons export potassium and organic osmolytes over about **24–48 h** and keep their size, so symptoms are few. Hence **acute = < 48 h** and **chronic = > 48 h**. Kumar notes that overt neurological features are rare above 125 mmol/L and usually appear around 115 mmol/L or lower.

blocks.title: SIADH: diagnostic criteria (Davidson)
items: Low plasma Na (usually < 130 mmol/L) with **plasma osmolality < 275 mOsmol/kg**.
**Urine osmolality > 100 mOsmol/kg** (not maximally dilute).
**Urine Na > 30 mmol/L**.
Low-normal urea, creatinine and urate.
Clinically **euvolaemic**.
No adrenal, thyroid, pituitary or renal failure and **no recent diuretics**.

blocks.title: SIADH: causes
items: **Tumours**, classically small cell lung cancer.
**CNS**: stroke, head injury, infection (e.g. meningitis), psychosis, porphyria.
**Lung**: pneumonia, lung abscess, TB, obstructive lung disease.
**Drugs**: carbamazepine and other anticonvulsants, SSRIs and other antidepressants, antipsychotics, cytotoxics (vincristine, cyclophosphamide), oral hypoglycaemics, opiates, NSAIDs, thiazides.
Post-operative state; idiopathic.

blocks.title: Stepwise work-up
items: **Step 1 – is it real and hypotonic?** Exclude a drip-arm sample, pseudohyponatraemia (severe hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia; osmolality normal) and translocation from hyperglycaemia or mannitol. True hyponatraemia has osmolality < 275 mOsmol/kg.
**Step 2 – urine osmolality.** Below 100 mOsmol/kg means the kidney is diluting properly: too much water in (primary polydipsia) or too little solute (beer potomania, 'tea and toast' diet).
**Step 3 – volume status plus urine Na.** Hypovolaemic with urine Na < 30 → extrarenal loss (vomiting, diarrhoea, pancreatitis); > 30 → renal loss (diuretics, adrenal insufficiency).
Euvolaemic → SIADH or hypothyroidism. Fluid-overloaded → heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, or kidney disease.

blocks.text: **Measuring ADH does not help.** It is high in hypovolaemia and in heart failure or cirrhosis (non-osmotic release), sometimes higher than in SIADH. ADH is suppressed only in **primary polydipsia** and iatrogenic water overload.
In hyponatraemia without fluid overload, check **magnesium and potassium**: deficiency of either boosts ADH release and underlies much diuretic-associated hyponatraemia.

**Not all low sodium is hypotonic.** Pseudohyponatraemia (lipids or paraprotein) has a normal osmolality and needs no sodium treatment. Hyperglycaemia pulls water out of cells: Na falls about 3 mmol/L for each 100 mg/dL (≈ 5.5 mmol/L) rise in glucose.

**Urine Na cut-off differs between books.** Davidson uses **30 mmol/L** to separate extrarenal (< 30) from renal (> 30) sodium loss; Kumar & Clark, Kumar & Clark's Essentials and Step-Up use about 20 mmol/L. Use Davidson's 30 in the exam, and remember urine Na is unreliable while the patient is taking diuretics.

**SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion.** Rule out adrenal insufficiency (short Synacthen test), hypothyroidism, diuretics, GI or skin losses and kidney disease first. Then a **chest X-ray** looks for pneumonia or lung cancer.

blocks.note: Look at: the algorithm flow from hypotonicity to urine osmolality (< 100) to urine Na (30 mmol/L split) and volume status.

blocks.title: Treatment by situation
rows: **Hypertonic 3% NaCl**: commonly a **150 mL bolus over 20 min**, repeated once or twice according to neurology and the Na rise (Davidson). Kumar: aim for +4–6 mmol/L in the first 4 h; 1 mL/kg of 3% saline raises Na by about 1 mmol/L
Stop the loss; give **IV 0.9% saline**. Restoring volume switches off non-osmotic ADH
**Fluid restriction 600–1000 mL/24 h** and remove the trigger (e.g. the drug). Persistent SIADH: oral **urea 30–45 g/day** (a solute load) or **tolvaptan** (risk of overcorrection)
Treat the underlying disease, strict fluid restriction, cautious diuretics (K-sparing helpful with secondary hyperaldosteronism)

blocks.title: Vaptans (ADH antagonists)
items: Block V2 receptors (**tolvaptan**; **conivaptan** blocks V1A and V2) → pure water diuresis with no change in Na or K excretion.
Tolvaptan is approved for **euvolaemic hyponatraemia/SIADH**.
Specialist-initiated, with close (e.g. 6-hourly) Na checks, because Na can rise very fast.
Demeclocycline (an older ADH-blocking tetracycline) is now rarely used.

blocks.text: **Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS)**, formerly central pontine myelinolysis: in chronic hyponatraemia, brain cells have shed osmolytes. A sudden rise in plasma osmolality pulls water out of them, they shrink and **separate from their myelin**. The course is often **biphasic**: encephalopathy improves, then days later **spastic quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy, mutism** or respiratory arrest appear. Lesions are mainly pontine but also in the basal ganglia and internal capsule. **MRI** (T1 low, T2 high signal) may take 2 weeks or more to become abnormal. Treatment is supportive only, and damage is often permanent or fatal.

blocks.title: Who is at highest risk
items: **ODS** with over-rapid correction: alcohol excess, cirrhosis, malnutrition, **hypokalaemia**; also prior hypoxaemia.
**Hyponatraemic encephalopathy** in acute hyponatraemia: premenopausal women, children, and **hypoxaemic** patients (hypoxia is the strongest predictor of death).
Classic iatrogenic setting: generous **5% glucose after surgery**, with stress-driven ADH.

blocks.text: **Correction limits differ between books.** Davidson: in chronic asymptomatic hyponatraemia raise Na by **no more than 10 mmol/L per 24 h**, and slower is safer. Kumar & Clark and Step-Up: **no more than 8 mmol/L per day** (lower still in high-risk patients). Use Davidson's figure in the exam; a slower target is never wrong.

**Overcorrection usually comes from a sudden water diuresis** once the ADH stimulus goes: volume is replaced, cortisol is given in Addison's, or nausea and pain settle. **Desmopressin** stops the diuresis, and 5% glucose can bring Na back down.
**Potassium replacement raises sodium.** In chronic hyponatraemia with severe hypokalaemia (e.g. Na < 120, K < 2 mmol/L), giving KCl alone can push Na up fast enough to cause ODS.

blocks.note: Look at: an abrupt osmolality fall (290 → 220) swells cerebral cells, while a gradual fall lets them lose osmolytes and keep a normal size.

blocks.text: **Hypernatraemia = serum Na > 145 mmol/L.** It means the kidney failed to concentrate urine while water intake was limited, or sodium was added. The usual cause is failure of the ADH system (**cranial or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus**); a low GFR or loop diuretic can also flatten the medullary gradient. Because thirst is so powerful, **sustained hypernatraemia implies blunted thirst or no access to water**: frail elderly people, neonates and unconscious patients.

blocks.title: Causes by volume status
rows: Osmotic diuretics, loop diuretic during water restriction, **glycosuria (hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state)**, colonic diarrhoea, heavy sweating
**Diabetes insipidus**: cranial, or nephrogenic (lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, tetracyclines, amphotericin B, acute tubular necrosis)
Enteral or parenteral feeding; IV or oral salt (hypertonic saline, **sodium bicarbonate** e.g. after cardiac arrest, high-Na drugs such as piperacillin); CKD with water restriction; Conn's, Cushing's

blocks.title: Clinical features (brain cell shrinkage)
items: Dizziness, restlessness, delirium and weakness.
Focal deficits and seizures, progressing to coma and death if water is not given.
Dry mucous membranes; worse when the rise is rapid.

blocks.title: Investigation: paired urine and plasma osmolality
rows: Urine **more dilute than plasma** despite a high Na
Kidney is working: **osmotic diuresis** or **extrarenal water loss** (sweat, heat stroke) or poor intake

blocks.title: Management
items: Treat the cause and **replace water**: orally if possible, or IV **5% dextrose or 0.45% saline**.
Davidson: if onset was rapid, start IV fluid at about **50–70 mL/h**; in elderly institutionalised patients (likely chronic) lower Na **very cautiously**.
**Hypovolaemic**: isotonic saline first to restore circulation, then free water.
**Cranial DI**: desmopressin. **Nephrogenic DI**: low-salt diet plus a thiazide, with adequate fluids.
**Hypervolaemic**: loop diuretic plus 5% dextrose; dialysis if in renal failure.

blocks.text: **Lowering Na too fast causes cerebral oedema.** Davidson gives no number, only caution. Kumar & Clark aim to correct over **about 48 h**; Step-Up caps the fall at about 12 mmol/L per day. Kumar & Clark's Essentials uses 0.9% saline (154 mmol/L) when Na exceeds 170 mmol/L, so that Na does not fall too steeply.

**Older people get both disorders.** As GFR declines they lose both diluting and concentrating ability. **Hyponatraemia** comes with low salt intake and thiazides; **hypernatraemia** with poor access to drinks, blunted thirst (advanced dementia, severe stroke) and high-sodium effervescent medicines.

**Hypokalaemia = serum K < 3.5 mmol/L** (normal about 3.6–5.0). About 98% of body potassium is inside cells, so shifts matter: **alkalosis, insulin, β2-agonists and aldosterone** push K into cells. The commonest chronic causes are **diuretics (especially thiazides)** and **hyperaldosteronism**. In hospital, K-free IV fluids and insulin treatment of DKA can drop K quickly.

blocks.title: Causes sorted by the clue
rows: Alkalosis, insulin, β-agonists, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis
Diarrhoea, laxative abuse, villous adenoma, fistula, ureterosigmoidostomy
Renal tubular acidosis types 1 and 2, acetazolamide

blocks.title: Inherited tubular causes compared
rows: K supplements, amiloride, rarely indometacin (biopsy: juxtaglomerular hyperplasia)
Amiloride or triamterene + salt restriction (spironolactone fails)

blocks.title: Clinical features
items: Mild (3.0–3.3 mmol/L): usually silent.
Weakness, tiredness and cramps; marked weakness below about 2.5 mmol/L; reduced reflexes.
Ventricular ectopics and arrhythmias; **digoxin toxicity potentiated** (more myocardial binding, less clearance).
Paralytic ileus.
Long-standing: hypokalaemic nephropathy and **acquired nephrogenic DI** (polyuria, polydipsia).
**ECG**: flattened (then inverted) T waves, **U waves**, ST depression.

blocks.title: Investigation
items: U&E, bicarbonate, urine K, and often Ca and Mg.
Urine K **> 30 mmol/24 h → renal** loss; **< 20 mmol/24 h → GI** loss (unless hypovolaemia has switched on aldosterone).
Plasma **renin low** → mineralocorticoid excess (e.g. Conn's); raised in other causes.
Unexplained alkalosis: **urine chloride < 30 mmol/L → vomiting**; > 40 mmol/L → diuretics or Bartter's/Gitelman's, separated by a **urine diuretic screen**.

blocks.title: Management
items: Treat the cause; reversing a shift may be enough.
Most patients: **oral slow-release KCl**.

IV KCl for severe hypokalaemia, arrhythmia, weakness, DKA or no oral route: Davidson generally **≤ 10 mmol/h**; peripheral fluid up to **40 mmol/L** in life-threatening cases; stronger solutions only via a central vein with cardiac monitoring.
Mix IV potassium in **0.9% saline, not glucose**; glucose triggers insulin and worsens the low K.
**Correct magnesium**, or K keeps leaking into the urine.
Amiloride can help when renal K loss is the cause.

blocks.text: **IV potassium rates vary by book.** Davidson: usually ≤ 10 mmol/h, ≤ 40 mmol/L peripherally. Step-Up: up to 10 mmol/h peripheral, 20 mmol/h central. Kumar & Clark's Essentials: above 20 mmol/h only with ECG monitoring and hourly K, and over 60 mmol/L irritates peripheral veins. Kumar: with poor renal function stay below 2 mmol/h. Quote Davidson in the exam.
**Refractory hypokalaemia → check magnesium.** Low cell magnesium drives ongoing tubular K secretion, so KCl alone fails until Mg is replaced.

blocks.note: Look at: the hypokalaemia ECG inset (U wave, ST depression) next to the hyperkalaemia inset (peaked T wave).

blocks.text: **Hyperkalaemia = serum K > 5 mmol/L.** First ask whether it is real. **Pseudohyperkalaemia** comes from haemolysis (difficult venepuncture, long tourniquet, fist clenching, delayed processing) or from K released by **platelets or white cells** during clotting in thrombocytosis or leucocytosis. Repeat the sample before treating, unless the ECG is abnormal.

blocks.title: True causes
rows: Acidosis (e.g. DKA), insulin lack, β-blockers, **rhabdomyolysis**, tumour lysis, severe haemolysis, suxamethonium, digoxin toxicity
**Addison's**, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, spironolactone/eplerenone, heparin, NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors, **type 4 RTA**
K supplements, K-containing fluids, stored blood

blocks.text: **Renal impairment plus drugs** is the commonest story. An ACE inhibitor combined with a K-sparing diuretic or an NSAID is especially dangerous: high K normally triggers aldosterone, which raises renal K excretion, and ACE inhibition blunts that loop.

blocks.title: Clinical features and ECG
items: Below about 6.5 mmol/L: usually silent.
Severe: progressive weakness, or **cardiac arrest with no warning**; Kussmaul breathing if acidotic; bradycardia, hypotension, asystole.
**ECG sequence**: tall peaked T waves → PR prolongation and flattening or loss of P waves → **broad QRS** → **sine-wave** pattern → VF or asystole.
Peaked T is early; QRS widening warns of imminent arrhythmia. A normal ECG does **not** exclude severe hyperkalaemia.

blocks.title: Emergency treatment (Davidson Box 14.17 with Kumar detail)
rows: Stabilises membranes; does **not** lower K; repeat if ECG changes persist
**Insulin + glucose** (50 mL 50% glucose); inhaled/nebulised **β2-agonist** (salbutamol); IV bicarbonate if acidotic
Insulin lowers K by about 1 mmol/L within an hour; check glucose for ≥ 6 h
Furosemide ± saline if kidneys work; K binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, older resins); **dialysis**
Dialysis is definitive in renal failure

blocks.text: **Insulin dose differs by source.** Davidson's box gives **5 IU soluble insulin (Actrapid)** with 50 mL 50% glucose; Kumar and Kumar & Clark's Essentials give **10 units**. Follow Davidson in the exam, and in every case monitor glucose for hypoglycaemia.

**When is it urgent?** Davidson: K above about **6.5–7.0 mmol/L**, or symptoms or ECG changes; below 6.5 without these, cut intake and fix causes. Zero to Finals: urgent at ≥ 6.5 regardless, or ≥ 6 with ECG changes. Kumar: above 7.0 is an emergency. Every patient with K > 6 needs an ECG.

**Resins and line safety.** Sodium polystyrene sulfonate lacks proven efficacy and has been linked to **intestinal necrosis**; newer binders are preferred. Never run bicarbonate in the same line as calcium (it precipitates), and give calcium cautiously to patients on digoxin.

blocks.title: Type 4 RTA and other links
items: **Type 4 RTA**: low aldosterone or aldosterone resistance (diabetes, ACE inhibitors, spironolactone, adrenal insufficiency, SLE) → **hyperkalaemia + hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis**; treated with fludrocortisone.
Hyperkalaemia itself reduces renal ammonia production, worsening acidosis and so worsening hyperkalaemia.
In aldosterone deficiency Na tends to be low: **exclude Addison's** unless another cause is obvious.
In **rhabdomyolysis**, K is the most immediately dangerous released product: check U&E and ECG early.

blocks.note: Look at: tented T waves, then small P waves with a widened QRS, then the sine-wave pattern before arrest.
Look at: the negative feedback loop: high K stimulates aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa, which raises renal K excretion.

cards.front: Total body water in a 70 kg man and how it is split?
cards.back: ≈ 40 L (60% of weight): ≈ 25 L intracellular, ≈ 15 L extracellular (≈ 12 L interstitial, ≈ 3 L plasma).

cards.front: What fraction of an infused litre stays in plasma: 5% dextrose vs 0.9% saline?
Daily adult maintenance per kg: water, Na, K?
cards.back: Water 35–45 mL/kg; Na 1.5–2 mmol/kg; K 1.0–1.5 mmol/kg.

cards.front: SIADH: plasma osmolality, urine osmolality and urine Na thresholds (Davidson)?
cards.back: Plasma osm < 275 mOsmol/kg; urine osm > 100 mOsmol/kg; urine Na > 30 mmol/L, in a euvolaemic patient off diuretics.

cards.front: Hyponatraemia with urine osmolality < 100 mOsmol/kg suggests?
cards.back: Excess water or too little solute: primary polydipsia, beer potomania, low-solute diet.

cards.front: Davidson's maximum rise in Na for chronic asymptomatic hyponatraemia?
cards.back: No more than 10 mmol/L per 24 h (slower is safer). Kumar & Clark: ≤ 8 mmol/L per day.

cards.front: Initial hypertonic saline for acute hyponatraemia with seizures (Davidson)?
cards.back: 3% NaCl 150 mL over 20 min, repeated once or twice depending on neurology and the Na rise.

cards.front: Hypernatraemia with dilute urine: how do you separate cranial from nephrogenic DI?
cards.back: Give desmopressin: urine concentrates → cranial DI; no response → nephrogenic DI.
Bartter's (loop-like, NKCC2): high urinary Ca. Gitelman's (thiazide-like, NCCT): low urinary Ca.

cards.front: Hypokalaemic alkalosis with urine chloride < 30 mmol/L points to?
cards.back: Vomiting (chloride lost as HCl). Urine Cl > 40 suggests diuretics or Bartter's/Gitelman's.

cards.front: Davidson's usual maximum rate of IV potassium?
cards.back: About 10 mmol/h; peripheral fluid up to 40 mmol/L in severe cases; higher only centrally with cardiac monitoring.

cards.front: First drug in severe hyperkalaemia, and does it lower K?
cards.back: 10 mL 10% calcium gluconate IV to stabilise the myocardium; it does not lower K.
Peaked T → PR lengthens and P waves flatten → broad QRS → sine wave → VF/asystole.
Haemolysis of the sample; thrombocytosis; leucocytosis (K released during clotting).

questions.stem: A 70 kg man who is bleeding from a duodenal ulcer is hypotensive. A junior doctor hangs 1 L of 5% dextrose to restore his blood pressure.
questions.leadIn: Approximately how much of this litre will remain in the plasma?
questions.explanation: Once the glucose is metabolised, the water spreads through all **40 L** of body water. Plasma is about **3 L**, so about **3/40** of the litre (≈ 75 mL) stays intravascular. That is why 5% dextrose is useless for resuscitation; use a crystalloid such as 0.9% saline.
whyNot: Too small: 3/40 of 1000 mL is about 75 mL, not 25 mL.
About 200 mL (≈ 3/15) is what 0.9% saline contributes, because it stays in the ECF.
No crystalloid keeps over half its volume in plasma; 5% dextrose keeps far less.
Only a fluid confined to the vessels could stay entirely in plasma; free water does not.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has been hiking for 8 hours in the heat without drinking. His plasma osmolality has risen and he passes a small volume of concentrated urine.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism directly allows his collecting ducts to reabsorb water?
options: ADH binding V1A receptors on vascular smooth muscle
ADH binding V2 receptors and inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane
Aldosterone opening epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct
Atrial natriuretic peptide increasing sodium excretion
Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl co-transporter in the thick ascending limb
questions.explanation: A rise in osmolality triggers posterior pituitary **ADH** release. ADH acts on **V2 receptors** in the collecting duct, which inserts **AQP-2** water channels so that water moves out along the medullary gradient (up to about 1200 mOsmol/kg).
whyNot: V1A receptors mediate vasoconstriction, not water reabsorption in the collecting duct.
Aldosterone retains sodium (water follows); it does not by itself make the collecting duct permeable to water.
ANP promotes natriuresis and would not concentrate the urine.
Blocking NKCC2 (as loop diuretics do) destroys the medullary gradient and impairs concentration.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man who smokes heavily has lost 6 kg over 3 months. He is mildly confused. He has a normal JVP, no oedema and no postural drop. He takes no regular medicines. Results: Na 121 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 254 mOsmol/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsmol/kg, urine Na 52 mmol/L. Thyroid function and a short Synacthen test are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: He is **euvolaemic** with true hypotonic hyponatraemia (osmolality < 275), **urine osmolality > 100** and **urine Na > 30**. Thyroid and adrenal causes are excluded and he takes no diuretics, so he meets the SIADH criteria. Weight loss in a smoker suggests a lung tumour, so get a chest X-ray next.
whyNot: Primary polydipsia gives a maximally dilute urine (osmolality < 100), not 480.
He takes no diuretics; thiazide hyponatraemia is also usually hypovolaemic.
Thyroid function is normal.
Pseudohyponatraemia has a normal plasma osmolality; his is low.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is admitted with acute pancreatitis. His blood sample looks milky. Laboratory Na is 126 mmol/L, measured plasma osmolality is 291 mOsmol/kg and glucose is normal. He has no neurological symptoms.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for the low sodium result?
questions.explanation: A low measured Na with a **normal osmolality** and a lipaemic sample means **pseudohyponatraemia**: lipid takes up part of the sample volume and the assay underestimates Na. Water balance is normal, so the sodium needs no treatment.
whyNot: SIADH causes true hypotonic hyponatraemia; osmolality would be below 275.
Glucose is normal, so there is no osmotic shift of water out of cells.
True hypovolaemic hyponatraemia would lower the measured osmolality.
Water excess lowers osmolality; his is normal.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol dependence was admitted with weeks of poor intake and Na 112 mmol/L. His Na rose to 129 mmol/L over the first 24 hours and his confusion improved. Four days later he develops slurred speech, difficulty swallowing and weakness of all four limbs with brisk reflexes.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic hyponatraemia was corrected by **17 mmol/L in 24 h**, well above Davidson's limit of 10. The **biphasic** course (improvement, then quadriparesis and pseudobulbar signs days later) is typical of **ODS**. Alcohol excess and malnutrition raise the risk. MRI may stay normal for 2 weeks or more.
whyNot: Wernicke's gives confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, not spastic quadriparesis with bulbar palsy after rapid Na correction.
His Na is now near normal and he had improved; cerebral oedema occurs with acute falls, not after correction.
Periodic paralysis is flaccid and episodic with hyporeflexia and is not linked to Na correction.
GBS causes ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia, not brisk reflexes and pseudobulbar palsy.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman had an appendicectomy yesterday and has received 3 L of 5% dextrose since. She has a generalised seizure. Na is 118 mmol/L (138 mmol/L before surgery). She is clinically euvolaemic.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Fluid restriction to 800 mL per 24 hours
questions.explanation: This is **acute** (< 48 h) iatrogenic hyponatraemia with **seizures**, i.e. cerebral oedema. Premenopausal women are at particular risk. Davidson: give **3% NaCl, 150 mL over 20 min**, repeated once or twice according to neurological response and Na rise. Rapid correction is safe here because the brain has not yet adapted.
whyNot: Fluid restriction works over days; it is too slow for seizures.
0.9% saline is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia; it cannot rapidly reverse cerebral oedema in a euvolaemic patient with seizures.
Tolvaptan is for chronic euvolaemic hyponatraemia, not emergency cerebral oedema.
Oral urea is used for persistent SIADH, not acute symptomatic hyponatraemia.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old woman with advanced dementia lives in a nursing home. She is drowsy with dry mucous membranes. Na is 162 mmol/L, glucose is normal and urine osmolality is 820 mOsmol/kg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely mechanism of her hypernatraemia?
options: Inadequate water intake from blunted thirst and poor access to drinks
questions.explanation: Her urine is **highly concentrated**, so ADH and the collecting duct are working: the kidney is saving water. The problem is **intake**. Advanced dementia blunts thirst and limits access to drinks, a classic setting for hypernatraemia in older people.
whyNot: Cranial DI gives dilute urine despite a high Na.
Nephrogenic DI also gives inappropriately dilute urine.
Conn's presents with hypertension and hypokalaemia; nothing here suggests it, and it does not explain water depletion with concentrated urine.
Nothing suggests she has received IV bicarbonate.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 15 years. She passes large volumes of urine and drinks constantly. After a day without access to water: Na 151 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 310 mOsmol/kg, urine osmolality 160 mOsmol/kg. After desmopressin, urine osmolality is 175 mOsmol/kg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Urine stays **more dilute than plasma** despite hypernatraemia, so this is diabetes insipidus. Urine barely changes after **desmopressin**, so the kidney is not responding to ADH: **nephrogenic** DI, a well-known effect of long-term **lithium**.
whyNot: In cranial DI the urine concentrates clearly after desmopressin.
Primary polydipsia causes low or normal Na, not hypernatraemia with dilute urine.
Osmotic diuresis produces urine of high osmolality.
SIADH causes hyponatraemia with concentrated urine.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with a low BMI is referred with fatigue. BP is 104/66 mmHg. She denies vomiting and takes no medicines. K is 2.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L and urine chloride 12 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her hypokalaemia?
questions.explanation: Normotensive hypokalaemic **alkalosis** has a short list: vomiting, diuretics, Bartter's or Gitelman's. A **urine chloride < 30 mmol/L** points to **vomiting**, because chloride is lost as gastric HCl. Diuretics and the tubulopathies give urine chloride above 40 mmol/L.
whyNot: Gitelman's gives a high urine chloride (> 40 mmol/L).
Laxative abuse causes hypokalaemia with metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.
Active diuretic use gives a high urine chloride; a urine diuretic screen would confirm it.
Conn's causes hypertension; her BP is low-normal.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man on a loop diuretic has K 2.6 mmol/L, proximal muscle weakness and frequent ventricular ectopics. He is vomiting and cannot take tablets. Renal function is normal and he has only a peripheral cannula.
questions.leadIn: Which IV prescription is most appropriate?
options: 40 mmol KCl in 1 L 0.9% saline over 4 hours
40 mmol KCl in 100 mL given over 10 minutes
40 mmol KCl in 1 L 5% dextrose over 4 hours
80 mmol KCl in 500 mL 0.9% saline over 1 hour
No potassium; give insulin and glucose
questions.explanation: This works out at **10 mmol/h** at **40 mmol/L**, Davidson's usual ceiling for a peripheral vein. It is given in **saline rather than glucose**. Check magnesium too, and monitor the ECG given the ectopics.
whyNot: A rapid concentrated bolus can cause fatal arrhythmia and is never given peripherally.
Glucose stimulates insulin, driving K into cells and worsening hypokalaemia.
80 mmol/h at 160 mmol/L is far above safe peripheral limits.
Insulin lowers K further; it treats hyperkalaemia.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with CKD stage 4 takes ramipril. He feels weak. K is 7.2 mmol/L and the ECG shows tall peaked T waves with a broadening QRS.
questions.leadIn: What should be given first?
options: Insulin with 50 mL of 50% glucose IV
questions.explanation: With severe hyperkalaemia and **ECG changes**, step one is **IV calcium gluconate** to stabilise the myocardium within minutes. It does not lower K. Then shift K into cells (insulin–glucose, β2-agonist) and finally remove it (binders, dialysis).
whyNot: Insulin–glucose is the next step; it takes longer to act and does not protect the heart immediately.
Salbutamol shifts K but comes after membrane stabilisation.
Resins act slowly, have doubtful efficacy and risk intestinal necrosis.
Dialysis may be needed but takes time to set up; protect the heart first.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with essential thrombocythaemia (platelets 1100 × 10⁹/L) has routine bloods. Serum K is 6.6 mmol/L. She feels well, takes no medicines, creatinine is normal and the ECG is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the potassium on a carefully taken sample, avoiding clotting and haemolysis
questions.explanation: A very high platelet count releases K during clotting, giving **pseudohyperkalaemia**. She is well, with normal renal function and a normal ECG. **Repeat the sample**, avoiding clotting and haemolysis, before any treatment.
whyNot: Calcium is for true severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.
Treating an artefact with insulin risks hypoglycaemia.
No binder is needed when the K is probably spurious.
Dialysis is grossly inappropriate for a likely artefact.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of hyponatraemia from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia is seen drinking water from taps throughout the day. He is euvolaemic. Na 124 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 258 mOsmol/kg, urine osmolality 70 mOsmol/kg.
items.explanation: Step 1: osmolality is low, so this is true hypotonic hyponatraemia. Step 2: urine osmolality is **below 100**, so the kidney is diluting maximally and ADH is switched off. Step 3: the history of heavy water drinking with a normal diet makes this **primary polydipsia** rather than low solute intake.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue, weight loss and darkening of her palmar creases. BP is 88/52 mmHg with a postural drop. Na 126 mmol/L, K 5.9 mmol/L, urine Na 58 mmol/L. She takes no medicines.
items.explanation: Step 1: she is **hypovolaemic**. Step 2: urine Na is **above 30**, so the kidney is losing salt; with no diuretic use, think **adrenal failure**. Step 3: **hyperkalaemia** and pigmentation confirm a lack of aldosterone and cortisol: **primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's)**.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman started a new tablet for hypertension 3 weeks ago. She is light-headed with dry mucosa and a postural drop. Na 123 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L, urine Na 46 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Step 1: **hypovolaemic** with **high urine Na**, so a renal salt loss. Step 2: the low K (not high, as in Addison's) plus a new antihypertensive points to a **thiazide**, the diuretic most likely to cause hyponatraemia, especially in older people.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man with a flare of Crohn's disease has passed 12 watery stools a day for a week. He has a postural drop and dry mucosa. Na 129 mmol/L, urine Na 8 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Step 1: **hypovolaemic**. Step 2: urine Na is **below 30**, so the kidneys are holding on to sodium appropriately and the loss is **extrarenal**. Step 3: profuse diarrhoea is the source: **GI sodium loss**. Treat with saline, which also switches off the non-osmotic ADH drive.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of hypokalaemia from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy has BP 168/100 mmHg. His father had hypertension from his twenties. K 2.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L. Plasma renin and aldosterone are both suppressed. BP and K improve on amiloride; spironolactone had no effect.
items.explanation: Hypertension and hypokalaemic alkalosis with **low renin and low aldosterone** means a mineralocorticoid-like effect without aldosterone. The family history and a response to **amiloride but not spironolactone** point to **Liddle's syndrome** (ENaC gain of function).

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with normal BP has cramps. K 3.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 31 mmol/L, magnesium low. Urinary calcium is low and urine chloride is 70 mmol/L. A urine diuretic screen is negative.
items.explanation: Normotensive hypokalaemic alkalosis with **high urine chloride** means diuretics or a tubulopathy. A **negative diuretic screen** leaves Bartter's or Gitelman's. **Low urinary calcium** and **low Mg** (a thiazide-like picture) point to **Gitelman's**.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man has hypertension that stays high on three drugs. K 3.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 31 mmol/L. Aldosterone is high and renin is suppressed. He eats no liquorice.
items.explanation: Hypertension with hypokalaemia and **high aldosterone with low renin** is **primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's)**. Liddle's and liquorice would suppress aldosterone.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with normal BP has K 2.9 mmol/L and bicarbonate 17 mmol/L. She denies bowel symptoms. 24-hour urine K is 11 mmol.
items.explanation: Two steps. **Low urine K** (< 20 mmol/24 h) means the kidney is conserving K, so the loss is **GI**, which rules out RTA (a renal cause). GI loss with **metabolic acidosis** comes from the lower gut; with the bowel symptoms denied, covert **laxative abuse** is the likely cause.

questions.theme: Management of sodium and water disorders
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most appropriate next treatment from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Fluid restriction to 600–1000 mL per day
Thiazide diuretic with a low-salt diet
Strict fluid restriction with cautious diuretic
No treatment of the sodium; repeat with measured osmolality

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman collapses after a marathon, having drunk large volumes of water throughout. She has a seizure in the emergency department. Na is 117 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Acute water intoxication (hours old) with **seizures** means cerebral oedema. Give **3% saline**, e.g. a 150 mL bolus over 20 min, repeated as needed. Rapid correction is safe because the brain has not adapted.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer. He is euvolaemic and asymptomatic, with Na 127 mmol/L that has fallen slowly over weeks. Investigations confirm SIADH.
items.explanation: This is chronic, asymptomatic euvolaemic hyponatraemia from SIADH. First-line treatment is **fluid restriction (600–1000 mL/day)** plus treating the cause. Avoid rapid correction.

items.stem: Six weeks later the same man's Na is still 124 mmol/L despite strict fluid restriction. The team wants an oral treatment that gives his kidneys extra solute to excrete water, avoiding the overcorrection risk of vasopressin antagonists.
items.explanation: For persistent SIADH Davidson lists **oral urea 30–45 g/day**, which provides a solute load that carries water out. Tolvaptan is the alternative but can overcorrect.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man who has taken lithium for years has polyuria and Na 148 mmol/L. His urine stayed dilute after desmopressin. Lithium cannot be stopped.
items.explanation: Two steps: no response to desmopressin means **nephrogenic DI**, so desmopressin is pointless. Nephrogenic DI is managed with a **low-salt diet and a thiazide**, plus adequate fluids.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of the raised potassium from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man with heart failure takes ramipril. Spironolactone was added 2 weeks ago. He is weak, K is 6.8 mmol/L and creatinine is slightly above his baseline.
items.explanation: An ACE inhibitor (less aldosterone) plus a mineralocorticoid antagonist (blocks aldosterone action), in an older patient with borderline renal function, is a classic dangerous combination for hyperkalaemia.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman is found on her kitchen floor after an estimated 2 days. Her urine is dark brown, CK is 85 000 U/L and K is 6.9 mmol/L.
items.explanation: A long lie, a very high CK and dark urine mean **rhabdomyolysis**. Muscle breakdown releases K, the most immediately dangerous product, often with AKI on top.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes and mild CKD has a persistent K of 5.9 mmol/L, a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with high chloride, and low renin and aldosterone. He takes no ACE inhibitor.
items.explanation: Two steps: hyperkalaemia plus **hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis** is the pattern of hyperkalaemic distal (**type 4**) RTA. Diabetes with **low renin and aldosterone** (hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism) is its typical cause.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man starts chemotherapy for a bulky high-grade lymphoma. Forty-eight hours later his K is 6.6 mmol/L and his urine output is falling.
items.explanation: Rapid destruction of a large, chemosensitive tumour soon after chemotherapy releases intracellular K: **tumour lysis syndrome**.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of hypernatraemia from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: Two days after transsphenoidal pituitary surgery, a 45-year-old woman passes 6 L of urine a day. Na 150 mmol/L, urine osmolality 110 mOsmol/kg. After desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 610 mOsmol/kg.
items.explanation: Dilute urine despite hypernatraemia means DI. A clear **rise after desmopressin** shows the kidney responds when ADH is supplied, so ADH production has failed: **cranial DI** after pituitary surgery.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is drowsy after a week of polyuria. Glucose 46 mmol/L, Na 156 mmol/L, ketones negative, urine osmolality high.
items.explanation: This is the hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state: **glycosuria** drives an osmotic diuresis that loses more water than sodium. The urine is concentrated, not dilute, which excludes DI.

items.stem: After a prolonged cardiac arrest, a 58-year-old man on ICU received repeated doses of IV sodium bicarbonate. He is now oedematous with Na 154 mmol/L.
items.explanation: **Hypervolaemic** hypernatraemia (oedema) after **sodium bicarbonate** means sodium was gained, not water lost: iatrogenic excess sodium administration.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with myeloma has corrected calcium 3.3 mmol/L, polyuria and Na 149 mmol/L. Urine osmolality is 190 mOsmol/kg and does not change after desmopressin.
items.explanation: Two steps: dilute urine that **does not respond to desmopressin** means nephrogenic DI. **Hypercalcaemia** is a recognised cause, here from myeloma.

questions.stem: A 70 kg man is nil by mouth for 24 hours after bowel surgery. He has no ongoing losses and normal electrolytes.
questions.leadIn: Which 24-hour IV prescription best meets his basic maintenance needs?
options: 2.5 L water, 120 mmol sodium, 80 mmol potassium
1 L water, 40 mmol sodium, 20 mmol potassium
5 L water, 300 mmol sodium, 200 mmol potassium
2.5 L water, no sodium, no potassium
3 L water, 460 mmol sodium, no potassium
questions.explanation: Davidson's maintenance: water **35–45 mL/kg** (≈ 2.45–3.15 L), Na **1.5–2 mmol/kg** (≈ 105–140 mmol), K **1–1.5 mmol/kg** (≈ 70–105 mmol). Only option A fits all three.
whyNot: Far too little water and electrolytes for a 70 kg adult.
About double every requirement; risks overload and hyperkalaemia.
Pure 5% dextrose gives no Na or K and risks hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia.
3 L of 0.9% saline gives about 460 mmol Na (over three times the need) and no potassium.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old woman from a care home has been drinking poorly for about 2 weeks. She is drowsy but haemodynamically stable. Na is 158 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: Which approach to correcting her sodium is most appropriate?
options: Hypotonic fluid (5% dextrose or 0.45% saline), lowering Na gradually over about 48 hours
5% dextrose at 1 L/hour to normalise Na within 12 hours
questions.explanation: This is probably **chronic** hypernatraemia from poor intake, so brain cells have adapted. Replace water with **5% dextrose or 0.45% saline** and lower Na **slowly** (over about 48 h). Davidson stresses extreme caution in older institutionalised patients.
whyNot: Rapid lowering of chronic hypernatraemia causes cerebral oedema.
Hypertonic saline would raise Na further.
Desmopressin treats cranial DI; there is no evidence of DI here.
A loop diuretic would worsen water loss in a dehydrated patient.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely disturbance or complication from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Cerebral oedema from over-rapid lowering of sodium

items.stem: A 76-year-old man takes digoxin and furosemide. He develops new frequent ventricular ectopics. His ECG shows prominent U waves and ST depression.
items.explanation: **U waves with ST depression** are the ECG signs of low K. A loop diuretic causes it, and hypokalaemia makes digoxin more arrhythmogenic.

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman admitted with Na 166 mmol/L after days of poor intake is given 5% dextrose fast. Her Na is 146 mmol/L 10 hours later, and she becomes more drowsy and then has a seizure.
items.explanation: Two steps: long-standing hypernatraemia means the brain has adapted, and a **20 mmol/L fall in 10 h** is far too fast. Water rushes into the brain cells, causing **cerebral oedema**.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with alcohol dependence and chronic diarrhoea has K 2.9 mmol/L. It barely rises despite 3 days of adequate oral and IV KCl.
items.explanation: **Refractory hypokalaemia** with alcohol excess and diarrhoea suggests **low magnesium**, which keeps renal K secretion going. Replace Mg and the K will correct.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman on haemodialysis misses a session and arrives with K 7.0 mmol/L and peaked T waves. Calcium gluconate has been given and the ECG has improved.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment works mainly by moving potassium into cells?
questions.explanation: **Insulin** drives K into cells via Na,K-ATPase; glucose prevents hypoglycaemia. It lowers K by about 1 mmol/L within an hour. Davidson uses 5 IU Actrapid, while Kumar and Kumar & Clark's Essentials use 10 units. β2-agonists and bicarbonate (if acidotic) also shift K.
whyNot: Calcium stabilises the myocardium but does not change the K level.
Resins remove K from the body via the gut, slowly.
Furosemide removes K in the urine (and she is dialysis-dependent).
Dialysis removes K from the body; it is definitive but not a shift.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most useful next investigation from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 69-year-old smoker has euvolaemic hyponatraemia (Na 123 mmol/L) with concentrated urine and urine Na 60 mmol/L. Thyroid function and a short Synacthen test are normal and he takes no diuretics.
items.explanation: The SIADH criteria are met once thyroid and adrenal causes are excluded. The next step is to find the cause; in a smoker, a **chest X-ray** looks for lung cancer or pneumonia.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with CKD stage 4 has a routine potassium of 6.4 mmol/L reported by phone. He feels well.
items.explanation: Every patient with K above 6 mmol/L needs an **ECG** straight away; ECG changes make treatment urgent.

items.stem: A 23-year-old normotensive woman has K 2.8 mmol/L and bicarbonate 33 mmol/L. Urine chloride is 68 mmol/L. She denies taking any medicines, and the team must separate a hidden drug from an inherited tubulopathy.
items.explanation: Two steps: high urine chloride in hypokalaemic alkalosis means **diuretics or Bartter's/Gitelman's**. The way to tell covert diuretic use from a primary tubular disorder is a **urine diuretic screen**.

ospe.identify: Two ECG insets: **peaked T wave** = hyperkalaemia; **U wave with ST depression** = hypokalaemia.
Progressive hyperkalaemia: tented T waves → reduced P waves with a widened QRS → sine-wave pattern before cardiac arrest.
Panel D **sine-wave** pattern = pre-arrest hyperkalaemia; panel B tented T wave is the earliest change.

Brain cells in hyponatraemia: abrupt osmolality fall → **swollen cells (cerebral oedema)**; gradual fall → osmolytes lost and **normal cell size**, which is why rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia is dangerous.
